fragile

/FRAJ-uhl/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Fragile means easily broken, damaged, or destroyed.

The movers wrapped the fragile antique mirror in three layers of padding before easing it down the narrow staircase.

Worked Example

The librarian turned the pages of the 400-year-old atlas with cotton gloves, because the fragile paper could crumble at a careless touch.

Paper that old is easily damaged — one rough touch could destroy it forever. That easy-to-ruin quality is exactly what fragile describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

breakable: Breakable states a plain fact: the thing can break without much force, so handle it with care — breakable ornaments, the breakable items in a moving box. Fragile goes further, suggesting the thing is likely to break and needs active protection. A mug is breakable; a hundred-year-old teacup is fragile.

flimsy: Flimsy means thin and weakly made — a flimsy folding chair, a flimsy excuse. It blames the construction: the thing was never sturdy to begin with. Fragile does not blame anyone; fine crystal is fragile by nature, not badly made. Flimsy things are cheap; fragile things are often precious.

frail: Frail means physically weak and easily harmed, and English reserves it mostly for people and living things — a frail patient, a frail elderly dog. Fragile is the word for objects and for figurative things like truces and egos. A frail grandmother may still own a fragile teacup.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

sturdy: strongly built

durable: able to withstand wear and rough use

Where it sits · how little stress it can survive — delicate → fragile → brittle

delicate vs. fragile: A delicate lace curtain needs gentle handling but survives careful use; a fragile one may break even when you are being careful.

brittle vs. fragile: Brittle goes further than fragile — a brittle object has grown so stiff and dry that it snaps or shatters at the slightest bend, while a fragile one simply breaks more easily than it should.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — frag

Root — frag: to break (Latin frangere)

Suffix — -ile

Suffix — -ile: tending to; able to

Put it together

Put it together: Something fragile is literally "able to break" — the same Latin frag/fract root hides inside fragment and fracture.

Use the root in a new word: fracture

Use the root in a new word: fracture: The X-ray showed a hairline fracture where the bone had cracked in the fall.

Word Choice

Neutral / everyday — also figurative

Fragile describes objects (fragile glassware, a fragile package) and, figuratively, things that could collapse at any moment — a fragile truce, fragile confidence, a fragile ecosystem. For a person's weak health, English usually prefers frail: a frail patient, but a fragile teacup.
